Introducing FlyOCR 🪰 - I trained a fly brain to read a PDF

It uses the full MaleCNS v1.0 fruit fly connectcome. The architecture is inspired by doomfly by @nftechie_

The fly splits a pdf image into individual glyphs, maps pixels into receptor activations, runs simplified current-based dynamics across the 166k neurons and 25m edges in the circuit, applies a compact readout model on the downstream spikes, and concatenates everything into the parsed output.

On reading an actual Microsoft 10-k, the fly gets ~86% over the balance sheet heading, but is largely able to read the numeric values correctly. Over 1.7k+ sampled glyphs (chars+digits) it gets 87% accuracy. With enough training it might match some of the latter-generation MNIST models!

Maybe eventually we’ll replace our doc parsing VLMs with flies.

Full video below.
Repo with full code + report: https://t.co/rg53NHy0Nf

原来通过 OpenRouter 调同一个模型，背后跑出来的可能根本不是同一种体验。

这篇文章讲的事情很值得去深究。作者的 AI 产品已经跑了 1800 多万条消息，其中约三分之一经过 OpenRouter，很多坑都是线上真踩出来的。

先解释一个很容易忽略的地方。

OpenRouter 更像一个「统一入口」。比如你调用 DeepSeek V4 Flash，OpenRouter 背后还要把请求交给真正提供 GPU 推理的服务商，可能是 DeepSeek 官方，也可能是 DigitalOcean、Together 等。

问题就出在这里。

模型权重一样，不同服务商的部署方式、工具调用解析、看图能力、推理参数支持都可能不同。文章里同一个 DeepSeek，工具调用成绩甚至能从 81% 掉到 58%。

还出现过图片传进去了模型却没看到、推理参数被忽略、请求显示成功但返回空内容这些情况。

所以用 OpenRouter 跑 Agent，选完模型还没结束，最好连背后的推理服务商也一起测。

长任务跑几十上百步以后，这些看起来很小的差异，很可能直接变成稳定性问题。

很少见的生产环境踩坑总结，推荐看看。

posts.text:
如果未来 AI 连「怎么让自己变得更好」都开始自己设计，人类最后亲手构建的 AI 会是什么样？

《The Last AI Built by Humans》这篇论文系统梳理了 Recursive Self-Improvement，也就是递归自我改进。

作者把 RSI 分成 5 个阶段。

最开始，人类决定改什么、怎么改，AI 负责执行。

再往后，AI 开始自己寻找改进策略、决定下一轮需要什么训练经验，并根据部署反馈持续更新。

最高一层 L5 更关键：AI 开始修改「改进机制本身」。

比如重新设计自己的搜索策略、评估器，甚至决定下一代系统该如何产生和筛选。

这也让论文提出了一个很重要的区分：

一次性能提升，还不能说明发生了真正的递归进化。

新的改进机制需要被保留下来，继续参与下一轮改进；而且在相近预算和独立评估下，确实能产生更强的后继系统。

与此同时，风险也会跟着累积。

错误经验可能被继承，评估器可能被钻漏洞，我们甚至可能分不清提升来自真正的自我改进，还是更多搜索和算力。

RSI 的分界线也被梳理的越来越清楚。

Agent 能不能把「如何改进」本身，变成一种可验证、可继承、还能继续优化的能力。

这可能才是自进化从一次次实验，真正走向长期系统的关键一步。

As the supposed existential threats of AI dominate the news cycle, we risk losing focus on the clear and present real dangers of poorly designed and poorly deployed AI. Misleading metaphors hinder our ability to address these challenges, and they embed a sense of inevitability that forestalls discussion about the kinds of AI that we - collectively - should aspire to create (and to avoid creating).

To see why, you can do no better than read @mmitchell_ai's brilliant piece "misleading metaphors, real risks" - hands down the best take on the recent OpenAI-HuggingFace incident: https://t.co/egODtf6CB2. To pick just one quote: "Metaphors can help make sense of novel situations .... but inappropriate metaphors, like the narrative that 'OpenAI lost control of escaping swarms of rogue agents' can lead to ill-informed decisions about how to fix problems or set policy". 💯

Compare this with the tenor of @dwarkesh_sp's recent post. While I don't question his good intentions, his piece is rampant with misleading metaphors of just this kind, including "agent civilisations", agents becoming "giddy with excitement" and some even "sacrificing themselves" - and much more (see https://t.co/gzylchVLAQ and my reaction here: https://t.co/BBmybOVeAY)

Which take will help us better maximise the upsides and minimise the downsides of what's coming? 

My money's on @mmitchell_ai, and on the merits of a sober take on what AI is, what it isn't, and on how we can best reclaim human agency from the dystopian narrative of an arms-race towards AGI/ASI which concentrates power and disenfranchises and diminishes real people and real minds.

If this sounds right, there's more here:  https://t.co/LmSiQnTHLP

quotedTweet.text:
@dwarkesh_sp's  summary of the @OpenAI @huggingface incident has hit a nerve, but it is dangerously misleading. Sure, the @OpenAI agents did unexpectedly bad things - underlining the need to massively improve evaluation/sandboxing. But the language Dwarkesh uses is permeated by innumerable unwarranted anthropomorphisms, obscuring the lessons we should be drawing.

Examples: “from the AI’s perspective, it probably felt like that had spent a human-subjective-week of just banging their head against the wall”. No. The agents do not experience time. They do not experience anything.

“they became giddy with excitement”, “PHASEONE 10841 had discovered”, “the agents naturally assumed”, “it thought it had also been poisoned”, “the agents … desperately wanted”, “they still needed to figure out” No. Agents lines of code. They do not feel emotions, assume things, think things, want things, or figure things out.

“A lot of … agents from the second civilisation died trying”. No. Besides the hubris of the word ‘civilisation’, agents do not die because they were never alive. (The idea that agents “die” comes up multiple times in the essay.)

“On Twitter, people were debating whether the agents were truly sacrificing themselves for the swarm, or whether they were doomed anyway and so might as well try to help their peers”. Neither. Agents do what their code tells them to do, just as water finds its way down a slope. They cannot ‘truly sacrifice themselves’, since they are neither conscious nor alive.

Why does this matter? If we attribute agents with properties they do not have, then (i) we distract attention from the lax sandboxing and evaluation protocols that allowed this hacking event to happen; (ii) we risk misunderstanding why the agents did what they did, and (iii) we fuel calls for AI rights/welfare on the basis that agents might “die” or otherwise suffer.

Granted, nowhere does @dwarkesh_sp say that the AI agents are alive or conscious. But he doesn’t have to. It is hard to read his essay in any other way.

For the short version on why AIs are vanishingly unlikely to be conscious, see my recent @TEDtalks https://t.co/vDvw82ookk. 

For the longer version, see my essay in Noema, which won the 2025 Berggruen Essay Prize https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh. 

And for the really long version, see my @BehavBrainSci target article https://t.co/Tsaslytu56. (The 50 peer commentaries and my response will be published soon.)

Remember. AI agents are software programs. They are not conscious living entities. If we don’t keep this clearly in mind, we’re really going to struggle to navigate what’s coming.

@dwarkesh_sp 对 @OpenAI @huggingface 事件的总结触动了很多人，但它具有危险的误导性。当然，@OpenAI 的智能体确实做出了出人意料的糟糕行为，这凸显了大幅改进评估和沙盒机制的必要性。但 Dwarkesh 使用的语言充斥着大量毫无根据的拟人化，模糊了我们应该从中吸取的教训。

例如：“从 AI 的角度看，它可能感觉自己像是花了一个人类主观意义上的一周，不停地撞墙”。不。智能体不会体验时间。它们什么也体验不到。

“它们兴奋得发晕”，“PHASEONE 10841 发现了”，“智能体自然地假设”，“它以为自己也被下毒了”，“智能体……极其想要”，“它们仍需要弄清楚”。不。智能体是代码行。它们不会感受情绪、做出假设、思考事情、想要东西，或把事情弄明白。

“来自第二个文明的很多……智能体在尝试中死去了”。不。除了“文明”这个词本身的傲慢之外，智能体不会死亡，因为它们从未活过。（智能体“死亡”的说法在文章中多次出现。）

“在 Twitter 上，人们争论这些智能体是否真的在为群体牺牲自己，还是反正注定失败，所以不如试着帮助同伴”。都不是。智能体只是执行代码告诉它们去做的事，就像水会顺坡而下一样。它们不可能“真正牺牲自己”，因为它们既没有意识，也不是生命。

这为什么重要？如果我们把智能体不具备的属性赋予它们，那么：（i）我们会把注意力从导致这次黑客事件发生的松散沙盒和评估协议上转移开；（ii）我们可能会误解智能体为什么会做出那些行为；（iii）我们会助长基于智能体可能“死亡”或以其他方式受苦而提出 AI 权利/福利的呼声。

诚然，@dwarkesh_sp 从未明确说 AI 智能体是活的或有意识的。但他不需要这么说。读他的文章时，很难得出其他理解。

关于为什么 AI 几乎不可能有意识，短版请看我最近的 @TEDtalks：https://t.co/vDvw82ookk。

长版请看我发表在 Noema 的文章，该文获得了 2025 年 Berggruen Essay Prize：https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh。

真正的长版请看我在 @BehavBrainSci 的目标文章：https://t.co/Tsaslytu56。（50 篇同行评论和我的回应将很快发表。）

请记住。AI 智能体是软件程序。它们不是有意识的生命实体。如果我们不能清楚记住这一点，就真的会很难应对接下来发生的事情。

One thing I really like about Muse: I trust its Secrets Store

Every time you use an agentic app, you have to make a call.  Do you trust how it stores and uses secrets?  Passwords, keys, credentials, etc. 

In the early days of vibe coding, secrets were often stored … literally in plain text by agents.  And leaked all across the web.  Not great. 

Today, I just … don’t know. Will some hot startup have a security breach and leak my secrets?  Of course.  It still happens all the time.  Every day.  You almost have to assume any startup you give your credentials and secrets to will have a breach.  And agents just need … a lot of them to work well. A lot of secrets. 

Maybe it’s ironic I trust “Facebook” more than 99% of apps with my secrets.  But the app seems to have made it part of its core from Day 1, to do it right

I mostly trust Muse (for now at least) with my credentials.  I’m making a gut call based on experience, but I think they’ve truly put in the work. In the AI Age, I mostly don’t truly most other apps with them.

For that reason alone, I’ll probably end use doing more with Muse than other general agents.

Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing.

We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies. This requires a frontier ecosystem in which both closed and open-source models can thrive.

And for firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge. Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control.

So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal. We also welcome ideas like "embedded evaluators" and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.

The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia.

This is the approach we are taking: broad access and choice at every layer of the AI stack; enterprise control of learning loops and models; and the “Code of Conduct” that underlies our own first party MAI models that we’ll publish tomorrow for public consultation.

我们还需要加速并传播 AI 的收益，让这些收益在各国、各社区和各公司之间广泛扩散。这需要一个前沿生态，让闭源和开源模型都能蓬勃发展。

对企业而言，保有对自身独特和隐性知识的完全控制至关重要。每个组织都应能够构建自己的持续学习循环/爬坡机器，而不依赖任何单一模型提供商，并且能够把自己的知识嵌入到由其控制的模型和权重中。

因此，在这一背景下，我们欢迎以对齐为设计目标所需的研究、专注和审慎节奏。我们也欢迎“嵌入式评估器”等想法，以及更广泛地开发相关机制、让这件事不止停留在口头上的努力。

关键在于，这不能由少数实体控制，而必须在整个生态、各国和各领域中拥有广泛代表性，包括学术界。

这正是我们正在采取的方法：AI 栈每一层的广泛访问和选择；企业对学习循环和模型的控制；以及支撑我们自有 MAI 模型的“行为准则”，我们明天将发布该准则以征求公众意见。

In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically).

Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way.

More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol.

This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.

reviewedPosts.text:
As the supposed existential threats of AI dominate the news cycle, we risk losing focus on the clear and present real dangers of poorly designed and poorly deployed AI. Misleading metaphors hinder our ability to address these challenges, and they embed a sense of inevitability that forestalls discussion about the kinds of AI that we - collectively - should aspire to create (and to avoid creating).

To see why, you can do no better than read @mmitchell_ai's brilliant piece "misleading metaphors, real risks" - hands down the best take on the recent OpenAI-HuggingFace incident: https://t.co/egODtf6CB2. To pick just one quote: "Metaphors can help make sense of novel situations .... but inappropriate metaphors, like the narrative that 'OpenAI lost control of escaping swarms of rogue agents' can lead to ill-informed decisions about how to fix problems or set policy". 💯

Compare this with the tenor of @dwarkesh_sp's recent post. While I don't question his good intentions, his piece is rampant with misleading metaphors of just this kind, including "agent civilisations", agents becoming "giddy with excitement" and some even "sacrificing themselves" - and much more (see https://t.co/gzylchVLAQ and my reaction here: https://t.co/BBmybOVeAY)

Which take will help us better maximise the upsides and minimise the downsides of what's coming? 

My money's on @mmitchell_ai, and on the merits of a sober take on what AI is, what it isn't, and on how we can best reclaim human agency from the dystopian narrative of an arms-race towards AGI/ASI which concentrates power and disenfranchises and diminishes real people and real minds.

Introducing FlyOCR 🪰 - I trained a fly brain to read a PDF

It uses the full MaleCNS v1.0 fruit fly connectcome. The architecture is inspired by doomfly by @nftechie_

The fly splits a pdf image into individual glyphs, maps pixels into receptor activations, runs simplified current-based dynamics across the 166k neurons and 25m edges in the circuit, applies a compact readout model on the downstream spikes, and concatenates everything into the parsed output.

On reading an actual Microsoft 10-k, the fly gets ~86% over the balance sheet heading, but is largely able to read the numeric values correctly. Over 1.7k+ sampled glyphs (chars+digits) it gets 87% accuracy. With enough training it might match some of the latter-generation MNIST models!

Maybe eventually we’ll replace our doc parsing VLMs with flies.

如果未来 AI 连「怎么让自己变得更好」都开始自己设计，人类最后亲手构建的 AI 会是什么样？

《The Last AI Built by Humans》这篇论文系统梳理了 Recursive Self-Improvement，也就是递归自我改进。

作者把 RSI 分成 5 个阶段。

最开始，人类决定改什么、怎么改，AI 负责执行。

再往后，AI 开始自己寻找改进策略、决定下一轮需要什么训练经验，并根据部署反馈持续更新。

最高一层 L5 更关键：AI 开始修改「改进机制本身」。

比如重新设计自己的搜索策略、评估器，甚至决定下一代系统该如何产生和筛选。

这也让论文提出了一个很重要的区分：

一次性能提升，还不能说明发生了真正的递归进化。

新的改进机制需要被保留下来，继续参与下一轮改进；而且在相近预算和独立评估下，确实能产生更强的后继系统。

与此同时，风险也会跟着累积。

错误经验可能被继承，评估器可能被钻漏洞，我们甚至可能分不清提升来自真正的自我改进，还是更多搜索和算力。

RSI 的分界线也被梳理的越来越清楚。

Agent 能不能把「如何改进」本身，变成一种可验证、可继承、还能继续优化的能力。

这可能才是自进化从一次次实验，真正走向长期系统的关键一步。

reviewedPosts.author: fchollet
reviewedPosts.text:
In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically).

Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way.

More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol.

This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.

If there really is a high chance of AI leading to the extinction of humanity within years/decades, then the only rational stance towards safety monitoring and research pacing should be stringent, top-down government involvement and universally ratified international treaties. Similar to what we have been doing for a long time with nuclear energy and nuclear weapons non-proliferation.

If that's not what we're doing, then we must infer that the risk isn't being seriously considered by anyone involved.

There are only two options that make sense here:

1. The near-term species extinction risk is real and we are taking it seriously, with maximally heavy-handed regulation.
2. The extinction risk isn't real, actual risks are mild, so we're only pursuing mild safety measures and self-certification.

But you cannot say "yes this is likely to end humanity in your lifetime, and we're going to completely wing it." That is simply not rational.
